title: A razor in its case
hookLine: the self fills you to the fingertips, hidden like fire in wood
carry: the mind is only one name of the self
tomorrow: dearer than a child, dearer than money. what could that be?

cards: Pick up a pencil case, a closed jar, a matchbox. Give it a shake: something's in there, and you can't see it. A few lines before aham brahmasmi, the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad reaches for objects just like that.
A razor, folded away in its case. Fire, asleep in a piece of wood. Footprints in soft ground.
Each one answers a question: where is the self, and why is it so easy to miss?

teach.h: TO THE TIPS OF THE FINGERNAILS.
teach.b: The text says the self has entered into all this, right to the tips of the fingernails.

teach.h: A RAZOR IN ITS CASE, FIRE IN WOOD.
teach.b: It's there the way a razor is there in its case, or fire in the wood it sleeps in. You can hold the case and never see the blade. You can hold the log and never see the flame.
Then the text says why people miss it. They see it in pieces. When it breathes, they call it breath.
When it speaks, voice. When it sees, the eye; when it hears, the ear; when it thinks, the mind.
These, the Upanishad says, are only names for what it does. Whoever holds on to just one of them doesn't know it whole.

Vedanta teachers draw the plain Hindu lesson from this: you, the atman, aren't your breath or your voice, or even your thoughts. Those are what the self does. So: know it as the self, for in the self all these become one.

This self, the text says, is the footprint of everything, because by it one knows everything, the way someone finds what was lost by following its tracks. The self isn't one more thing to go and find.

teach.h: THE TRAIL ALL ELSE IS FOUND BY.
teach.b: It's the trail everything else is found by. And aham brahmasmi says that this same self, in the case, in the wood, on the trail, is Brahman.

how: Students of the Brihadaranyaka read these pictures, the razor, the fire in wood and the footprint, with a teacher as the setting for aham brahmasmi.

o: I hide Brahman: a secret kept by sages
I find Brahman: a prize at a journey's end
I am Brahman: the self is the one reality

games.q: three pictures of the self. tap the pairs.
p: only names for what it does
the trail everything is found by

s: in this text the self lives in one spot, like the heart or the head
it has entered everything to the tips of the nails, like a razor in its case.
the Brihadaranyaka calls the self the footprint of everything
by it one knows everything, the way one finds what was lost by its tracks.
breath, voice, eye and mind are each the whole self
they're names for what it does; whoever holds just one doesn't know it whole.

games.q: a friend says: 'i'm my anxious thoughts. that's just who i am.' by the Brihadaranyaka's picture, what's going on?
o: thinking is one name for what the self does; holding one name misses the whole.
right: whatever you think about most is the whole self.
thoughts are fake, so the self has nothing to do with them.
games.why: when it thinks, it's called mind. these are only names of its acts, the text says; whoever holds just one doesn't know it whole.

practice: Hold one closed thing near you: a box, a jar, a book. Feel its weight and its edges with your eyes open, and know there's something in it you can't see.
Then turn the same attention to the hand holding it, all the way to the fingertips.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi, and where its self is: in everything to the fingertips, like a razor in its case, and the trail all else is found by.

orig.note: Sanskrit padaniyam, the footprint, the trail: 'this self is the footprint of all this'.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the mind is only one name of the self, hidden like fire in the wood. That's day 1747.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.7 (the self entered here to the tips of the nails, as a razor in its case or fire in its source; breathing it is called breath, speaking voice, seeing the eye, hearing the ear, thinking the mind: these are only names of its acts; whoever worships one of these does not know; it should be known as the self, for in it all these become one; this self is the footprint of all this, for by it one knows all this, as one finds by footprints)
